Senses.Explanation: The phrase marks a person's immediate descent from the formal teaching seat and thereby closes or interrupts a hall event. Shakyamuni descends after Manjusri's sounding-block verse; Linji descends after Magu leaves their disrupted exchange; Mazu descends when Baizhang rolls up the mat just after he has mounted the seat; and Feiyin ends an admonitory address in the same way. Senses.Explanation: Then shouted marks a shout as the immediate next act in an encounter; 便 contributes sequence and promptness, while 喝 names the vocal action. Distinct higher-tier records conserve Deshan Xuanjian's shout as Guishan Lingyou reaches for his whisk, Linji Yixuan's shout when a monk hesitates, and an unnamed monk's shout after Yushan strikes him. Yeyun Ying's lineage verse preserves the inherited Xinghua Cunjiang event with Sansheng Huiran; Yuanwu Keqin later actively raises and appraises an inherited Xinghua encounter in which the participants answer shout with shout. These are related family presentations, not two original Xinghua events. The phrase reports timing and action rather than a fixed force carried by every shout. Jade Flowers remains the sole supplementary lamp recension, preserving an unnamed monk's immediate shout before Yangshan Huiji.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB309.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunfu Daozhi, a reply letter to a layman studying the Huayan. Yunfu Daozhi owns the letter deployment: at a time when the ancestral lamp is scattered he recounts how the Huayan master Zujue first mastered the Huayan and lectured unmatched through the southwest, was told by Nantang Jing he had not yet shed the mark of the written word, and went south to Yuanwu; one day entering the room Yuanwu raised Luoshan's couplet — with words, sit firm on the tiger's head and gather its tail, the purpose shown beneath the first sentence; wordless, the pivotal edge flashes bare like a lightning-swift brush — how do you take it? Zujue could not answer, strove day and night to a sudden awakening, sent Yuanwu the verse of the lone peak's summit and the half-shut gate, and was approved; pressed again the next day he was shouted down — this is not the truth of the teaching — stayed five years more in muddle, until reading Fushan Yuan's treatise on cutting away attachment at Qixian on Lu, that in a sandalwood grove no foul weed grows, he broke through, sent the verse of coming out of the grove back into the weeds, and Yuanwu held it up before the assembly: the Huayan master is through. Yunfu closes the letter: that Jue would not rest content, and Yuanwu's carrying him to the end — this the layman too should know.
